content: Superficial thrombophlebitis of the upper extremity is a common complication associated with the use of intravenous catheters in peripheral veins, particularly in the forearm or hand. Despite its frequency, there is no established consensus on the optimal management of this condition in clinical practice. The objective of this review was to evaluate evidence from randomized clinical trials (RCTs) regarding the efficacy and safety of various medical treatments—whether topical, oral, or parenteral—for superficial thrombophlebitis of the upper extremity. The search for relevant studies included databases such as the Cochrane Vascular Group Specialised Register and the Cochrane Register of Studies, with the last search conducted in April 2015. Clinical trial registries were also reviewed up to the same date. The inclusion criteria for the review were RCTs that compared any form of medical treatment (topical, oral, or parenteral) to either no intervention or placebo, or that compared different medical interventions, such as variations in treatment regimens or pharmacological types. Data were extracted on methodological quality, patient characteristics, interventions, and outcomes. The primary outcomes assessed were the improvement of signs and symptoms (effectiveness) and the occurrence of side effects (safety). Thirteen studies involving a total of 917 participants were identified. The treatments evaluated included topical therapies (11 studies), oral therapies (2 studies), and parenteral therapies (2 studies). Seven studies included a placebo or no-intervention control group, while the remaining studies compared active treatment groups. None of the studies investigated the effects of ice application or the use of cold or hot bandages. The risk of bias in the included studies was generally moderate to high, and poor reporting limited the ability to fully assess the risk of bias in many cases. The overall quality of evidence for the outcomes ranged from low to moderate, primarily due to issues with bias and imprecision. Most comparisons were based on single trials, and differences in study designs, outcomes, and measurement tools precluded statistical pooling of data for the primary outcomes. Topical treatments, such as heparinoid or diclofenac gels, were found to reduce pain compared to placebo or no intervention. Oral non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) were shown to decrease the intensity of signs and symptoms when compared to placebo. However, safety data were inconsistently reported and were unavailable for certain interventions, such as notoginseng creams, parenteral low-molecular-weight heparin, or defibrotide. Adverse events associated with topical treatments, such as heparinoid creams, Essaven gel, or phlebolan, were reported in some trials but were primarily limited to local allergic reactions. These trials were underpowered to detect significant differences in adverse events between treatment modalities. Only one small study, involving 15 participants, assessed thrombus extension and symptomatic venous thromboembolism in patients treated with either oral NSAIDs or low-molecular-weight heparin. This study reported no cases of thrombus extension or venous thromboembolism. No studies reported on the development of suppurative phlebitis, catheter-related bloodstream infections, or quality of life outcomes. In conclusion, the evidence regarding the treatment of acute superficial infusion thrombophlebitis is limited and of low quality. The available data are insufficient to draw definitive conclusions about the effectiveness and safety of topical treatments, systemic anticoagulation, or oral NSAIDs for this condition. Further high-quality research is needed to guide clinical practice.
